title: Foundations: read, test, and choose a design pattern

opening.title: Design patterns: make the next change safer
keyPoints: 22 named patterns, one problem-solving method
Follow code, calls, ownership, and lifetime
Dr. Charles Dorner
opening.narration: Welcome to Design Patterns. Our job is to learn how to choose and defend an arrangement of code when a real requirement makes the current arrangement hard to change. A design pattern is a named solution structure for a recurring kind of problem. It is not a prize for using more classes. Throughout this course we will begin with working code, expose a specific limit, and then test a better arrangement. You will read C++ and diagrams together, predict what the program does, and explain what must remain true. Class 0 gives us the words and habits that make those later lessons useful.
actions: Open presenter notes for the spoken teaching script.
Ask learners to name one change that made an earlier program difficult to maintain.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.01: Teach the pattern, then test the design

question.prompt: What evidence makes a pattern worth introducing?
question.answer: A concrete requirement exposes a change or failure that the new arrangement makes easier to handle while preserving the program’s promises.

opening.title: What counts as understanding a pattern?
keyPoints: State its pressure before its name
Locate roles in actual C++
Predict success and failure paths
Reject the pattern when a simpler design fits
opening.narration: Knowing the name is the first step, not the final test. By the end of a chapter you should be able to describe the problem in ordinary words, identify each responsibility in code, and follow a request through the objects that take part. You should also explain a failure case and an alternative design. The strongest test is a changed requirement: can you place the change without breaking earlier behavior? A class diagram can look familiar while the code fails its contract. We will therefore treat names, diagrams, output, and tests as parts of one explanation, rather than four separate lists to memorize.

question.prompt: A learner draws the right boxes but cannot trace a call. What is still missing?
question.answer: The mechanism: which object receives each request, what data moves, and why the design preserves its promises.

opening.title: Pattern, algorithm, and library are different things
keyPoints: Algorithm: steps that compute a result
Pattern: responsibilities and relationships
Library: reusable implementation code
opening.narration: Imagine that a monitor must choose either an average or the highest reading. The steps for finding an average form an algorithm. The arrangement that lets the monitor use different algorithms through the same request may be Strategy. A standard library container, such as std::vector, is actual reusable code that stores the readings. These three things can appear in one program without meaning the same thing. A pattern does not give you a ready-made function to paste into every project. You must still choose data types, ownership rules, failure behavior, and tests that fit your program. That adaptation is where design judgment enters.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

question.prompt: Does using std::vector mean that a program uses the Strategy pattern?
question.answer: No. A container supplies code for storing values. Strategy concerns making a varying operation interchangeable behind an agreed request.

opening.title: Start with one requirement and one function
keyPoints: Two readings are known to lie from 0 through 1000
Report their integer mean
No interchangeable object is needed
opening.narration: Our first requirement is deliberately small. Two integer readings lie between zero and one thousand, and the program reports their integer mean. Integer division drops any fractional part, which is acceptable for this demonstration. The values two and eight therefore produce five. A function with two parameters is enough. Each parameter is a local value initialized from an argument at the call. The return statement gives the result back to main. We have no evidence yet that creating interfaces or rule objects would help. A clear precondition, a small calculation, and an exact output make this design easy to review.
actions: Predict the output before running the complete program.
Change the inputs to 3 and 8 and explain why the result becomes 5.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

question.prompt: What prints, and what assumption makes adding the two integers safe here?
question.answer: mean=5. Both inputs are restricted to 0 through 1000, so their sum is comfortably within the int range required by C++.

opening.title: A new requirement creates a design question
keyPoints: Some users need the highest reading
They must choose the rule during a run
Two stable branches may still be enough
opening.narration: Now users ask for the highest reading as well as the mean. That is a new requirement, not proof that the first function was badly written. For two stable choices, a small branch in one place can remain the best design. The pressure becomes stronger when several clients copy those branches, when rules change independently, or when a running program must replace its rule. Notice the order of our reasoning. We name the variation first: the estimate calculation. Then we ask where that variation currently spreads. Only after that do we compare a function parameter, an enum with a switch, and separate rule objects.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

question.prompt: Which question should come first: “Which pattern?” or “What must vary independently?”
question.answer: Ask what must vary independently. That identifies the pressure and gives a reason to compare particular patterns.

opening.title: A safe demonstration of duplicated decision logic
keyPoints: Dashboard and report both select a calculation
Only one caller learns about the highest rule
The program compiles but the answers disagree
opening.narration: This program has no dangling pointer and no mysterious crash. Its failure is easier to miss: two callers interpret the same request differently. The dashboard handles the highest rule, but the report still always computes the mean. For readings one and nine, the reviewed dashboard prints nine while the stale report prints five. Both calculations are valid C++, so compilation cannot identify the missing requirement. Keeping one shared function would already repair this small case. If independently replaceable rules become a lasting need, a Strategy boundary can keep both callers from owning their own copies of the rule-selection logic.
actions: Ask learners whether the compiler should reject this program.
Run it, then identify the earliest point at which the two callers assign different meaning to the request.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.04: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

question.prompt: Why does the stale report print 5 instead of 9?
question.answer: It ignores the requested rule and always uses the mean calculation. The missing highest branch is a behavioral defect, not a syntax error.

opening.title: Judge a boundary by the change it contains
keyPoints: Keep rule calculations together
Make callers depend on one meaningful request
Pay for extra structure only when it earns its place
opening.narration: A boundary is the point where one part of a program meets another through a defined agreement. In our estimate example, a good boundary says what inputs the calculation accepts and what result it returns. The dashboard should not need to know every step of every calculation. However, a boundary does not always need a base class. One shared function could remove the duplicated logic today. A function parameter could let a caller supply a calculation tomorrow. A virtual interface becomes useful when named rule objects, stored choices, or lifetime management matter. We compare these costs against real changes, not against a rule that advanced syntax is always better.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.06: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose

question.prompt: What is the smallest repair for the demonstrated drift?
question.answer: Use one shared selection/calculation implementation. Separate Strategy objects are justified only if the wider replacement and extension requirements warrant them.

comparisons.label: One shared function
comparisons.text: Best when the small set of choices is stable and centralized.

comparisons.label: Supplied operation
comparisons.text: Fits callers that need different calculations without an object family.

comparisons.label: Strategy objects
comparisons.text: Useful when named policies are stored, replaced, and extended behind a stable contract.

opening.title: The creation family asks who builds the object
keyPoints: Factory Method: vary one creation step
Abstract Factory: create compatible families
Builder, Prototype, Singleton: different creation pressures
opening.narration: The five creational patterns organize object creation. Factory Method lets a shared workflow ask a replaceable creation step for the object it needs. Abstract Factory keeps a family of related choices compatible. Builder makes a multi-step construction process clearer. Prototype creates a new object by copying an existing configuration with a stated copy policy. Singleton controls access to one instance, which also creates concerns about shared state and lifetime. These names do not describe five spellings of new. Each addresses a different pressure. During the chapters, we will ask what must be created, who decides its exact kind, and who owns the completed result.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

question.prompt: Why is “I need to create an object” too broad to select a creational pattern?
question.answer: All ordinary programs create objects. Selection depends on the particular pressure: a varying step, compatible family, staged construction, copying policy, or controlled instance.

opening.title: The structure family asks how parts fit together
keyPoints: Adapter translates; Bridge separates independent dimensions
Composite represents a tree; Decorator wraps behavior
Facade simplifies; Flyweight shares; Proxy controls access
opening.narration: The seven structural patterns organize how parts connect. Adapter changes the form of a request or value so two sides can work together. Bridge separates two dimensions that must vary independently. Composite treats a tree of parts through a common operation. Decorator adds behavior around another object. Facade offers a simpler entrance to a subsystem. Flyweight shares suitable common data. Proxy stands in front of another object to control access. Some of these diagrams contain a field that refers to another object, but that shared shape does not make the patterns identical. We must ask what the connection is for and what the caller is promised.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

question.prompt: Adapter and Decorator can both hold another object. What separates their purposes?
question.answer: Adapter translates an interface or representation. Decorator preserves an interface while adding behavior around the wrapped operation.

opening.title: The behavior family asks how work is shared
keyPoints: Route, record, traverse, coordinate, or remember work
Notify, switch state behavior, or replace an algorithm
Fix a workflow or add operations across a type family
opening.narration: The ten behavioral patterns organize decisions and cooperation. Chain of Responsibility routes requests along possible handlers. Command turns a request into something the program can store or schedule. Iterator traverses a collection without exposing its storage details. Mediator coordinates participants. Memento records restorable state. Observer notifies interested parties. State delegates behavior that depends on the current state. Strategy replaces an algorithm. Template Method fixes a workflow while allowing selected steps to vary. Visitor places related operations over a type family. You do not need to memorize every mechanism now. Keep the problem verbs as retrieval cues, then replace each short description with a code trace as we study the chapter.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.10: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change

question.prompt: Which clue points more directly to Strategy: “many objects” or “replace the calculation without changing the caller”?
question.answer: Replace the calculation without changing the caller. The number of objects alone says little about intent.

opening.title: One chapter follows a chain of evidence
keyPoints: Requirement → baseline → limitation
Mechanism → code → predicted output
Failure → repair → justified alternative
opening.narration: We will use the same learning process while changing the problems. First, state a requirement and its limits. Next, make the simplest reasonable version and identify a specific new need it cannot handle well. Then introduce the feature or pattern that addresses that limit. Follow the actual code and diagrams, predict output, and run checks. Finally, break one promise deliberately, repair it, and compare a plausible alternative. This sequence prevents a common mistake: learning a pattern as a diagram detached from its reason to exist. When you review, practice retelling that chain in your own words before looking at the chapter answer.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.01: Teach the pattern, then test the design

question.prompt: What should you say immediately before naming a pattern in a design review?
question.answer: State the requirement and the concrete limitation that motivates the proposed arrangement.

opening.title: A type is a rule; an object is a particular instance
keyPoints: Class: a user-defined type
Object: one instance with a lifetime
Member: data or a function declared inside the class
opening.narration: A type tells the compiler what kind of value we are using and which operations are allowed. A class is one way to define a type that groups data and functions. An object is a particular instance of a type: two monitors can use the same class while holding different readings. A member belongs to the class declaration; a member function is often called a method. Object lifetime is the period in which that particular object exists, from completed construction until destruction begins. Pattern diagrams usually show types, but a running program contains objects. Keep that difference in mind when a diagram shows one rule box and execution creates several rule instances.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.05: The object words used by the patterns

question.prompt: Does one Rule class box mean only one Rule object can exist?
question.answer: No. The box normally represents a type or role. Many objects can have that type, each with its own lifetime and state.

opening.title: A value parameter and a reference do different jobs
keyPoints: Value parameter: work on a separate parameter object
Reference: another name for an existing object
const reference: a borrowed view that cannot modify through that name
opening.narration: This example shows a mistake without causing unsafe memory access. add_to_copy receives a Tally value, so its change affects a separate parameter object. The tally in main remains five. add_to_original receives Tally followed by an ampersand, which declares a reference. The parameter is another name for the object in main, so adding three changes that object to eight. observe takes a const reference: it reads the same object while disallowing ordinary modification through that parameter. None of these calls transfers ownership. The original tally stays alive in main for all three calls, which makes the borrowed references valid.
actions: Predict both output lines before running.
Ask whether replacing a reference with a value is always a harmless optimization.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

question.prompt: Why are the printed counts 5 and then 8?
question.answer: The first function changes a value copy. The second changes the original through a reference. Both observations read the original tally.

opening.title: An invariant is a rule the boundary must preserve
keyPoints: Example: every monitor always has a usable rule
Private data blocks uncontrolled access
Every public operation must keep the rule true
opening.narration: An invariant is a rule that must remain true whenever a caller can observe the object at its public boundary. Suppose a monitor requires a usable estimate rule. Making its rule field private prevents ordinary outside code from directly clearing that field, but privacy alone is not enough. A public replace operation could still accept an empty owner and break the promise. A sound operation checks the proposed replacement before changing the current one. Encapsulation means placing related data and behavior behind a controlled boundary. The point is to make valid changes easy and invalid states hard to create, not merely to add the word private.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.05: The object words used by the patterns

question.prompt: A private rule pointer can be set to null by a public setter. Is the non-null invariant protected?
question.answer: No. Access control hides the field, but the public operation still allows a state that violates the contract.

opening.title: An interface includes promises, not just names
keyPoints: Precondition: what must hold before a call
Postcondition: what the call guarantees afterward
Invariant: what remains true at observable boundaries
opening.narration: An interface is the set of operations a caller may use together with the promises that give those operations meaning. An estimate function might require a nonempty list and guarantee a result within the range of its inputs. The nonempty rule is a precondition. The result guarantee is a postcondition. A permanently usable rule can be an object invariant. C++ function declarations describe types, but many of these value rules need written documentation and running checks. A function named estimate that silently returns Fahrenheit when callers expect Celsius can have the correct signature and still break the interface. Design begins with meaning before it becomes syntax.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.05: The object words used by the patterns

question.prompt: Two implementations have identical signatures. Are they automatically interchangeable?
question.answer: No. They must also preserve the same preconditions, result guarantees, units, lifetime assumptions, and other promised behavior.

opening.title: One request, two implementations
keyPoints: Estimate defines the common request
Mean and Highest provide different behavior
The owner can replace its rule between calls
opening.narration: Here the new requirement finally earns an interchangeable rule. Estimate declares a virtual operation named value. Mean and Highest supply concrete answers with the same input contract: integers from zero through one thousand. The owning pointer initially holds Mean, so the first call returns five for one and nine. Replacing it with Highest destroys the old owned rule and makes the next call return nine. Both calls use the same expression, rule followed by an arrow and value. Virtual dispatch selects the implementation associated with the actual object during execution. This small program demonstrates the mechanism that the Strategy chapter will examine in depth.
actions: Predict both calls and identify the actual object each time.
Trace what happens to the old Mean object at replacement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

question.prompt: The call expression stays the same. Why does the second result change?
question.answer: The owning pointer now holds a Highest object. The virtual call selects that object’s override instead of Mean’s override.

opening.title: Read the diagram against the running estimate
opening.eyebrow: CLASS 0 · ACTUAL CODE, TYPES, AND OWNERSHIP
keyPoints: Mean and Highest inherit the Estimate contract
The local rule handle owns one concrete object at a time
Replacement changes the object, not the call expression
Diagram code is excerpted from the preceding runnable program
opening.narration: Read this picture from the actual code rather than guessing from its shape. The purple block is main and its local owning handle, not another invented class. Its filled-diamond connection says that rule owns the current concrete object through Estimate. The blue class blocks each point a hollow triangle toward their common base, which means public inheritance. Initially the owner contains Mean; assignment replaces it with Highest and releases the old object. The virtual value declaration explains why the unchanged call selects a different implementation. Added comments begin with Teaching and explain the excerpt. They are annotations, not extra UML relationships or executable steps.
actions: Point to each diagram excerpt in the preceding complete program.
Trace ownership at construction, replacement, and the end of main.

question.prompt: Does the diagram say that Mean owns Estimate, or that Mean can be used through Estimate?
question.answer: Mean can be used through the Estimate contract. The hollow triangle indicates inheritance. The separate filled diamond is at the main-local rule owner and indicates exclusive ownership of the current concrete object.

visual.title: Replaceable estimate: actual class relationships and ownership
visual.caption: C++ excerpts come from the preceding dp_ch00_replaceable_estimate.cpp demonstration. Hollow triangles point from Mean and Highest to their public base Estimate. The filled diamond sits at the exclusive owner, the main-local unique_ptr named rule; it owns one concrete object at a time. Lines beginning // Teaching: are added teaching comments, not UML relationships. The other C++ lines are copied verbatim from the complete program. Use horizontal scrolling at intrinsic size when needed.

theory.what: Two concrete classes fulfill one virtual Estimate contract; main holds the exclusive owner of the currently selected object.
theory.where: Immediately after the complete replaceable-estimate demonstration. Each diagram code block is copied from that program; added explanatory comments are labeled Teaching.
theory.why: Callers need one request while the selected estimate changes during execution. The diagram separates substitution from ownership.
theory.invariant: The call uses a live non-null rule, and both implementations accept the stated integer input range. Each owned concrete object is destroyed exactly once.
theory.risk: A dangling borrowed pointer, an empty owner at a call, a missing virtual destructor, or an incorrect override body would break different parts of the contract.

opening.title: Read virtual, override, and const where they matter
keyPoints: virtual: permit dispatch through the base interface
override: ask the compiler to check the match
= 0: leave the operation abstract
const after the parameters: restrict changes through this call
opening.narration: In the preceding program, virtual marks a member function whose final override can be selected through a base reference or pointer. The equals zero after the declaration makes the operation pure virtual: Estimate does not provide a usable concrete answer there. Mean and Highest use override so the compiler rejects a mismatch with the base virtual function. The const after the parameter list applies to the receiving object through that call. It does not prove that the function has no possible outside effects. The colon in class Mean followed by public Estimate declares public inheritance. Here it means that a Mean can be used through the Estimate contract.

opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

question.prompt: Does override prove that Highest returns the highest reading?
question.answer: No. It verifies the virtual-function relationship and signature compatibility. The behavior still needs reasoning and tests.

opening.title: Access, ownership, and lifetime are separate facts
keyPoints: A pointer can give access without owning
unique_ptr has one owner of its object
A borrowed reference does not extend the target’s lifetime
opening.narration: Ownership means responsibility for ending a resource’s lifetime. A raw pointer can hold an address without saying who owns the object. A reference gives access to an existing object but does not normally keep it alive. In our rule demo, unique_ptr is an owning handle that releases the concrete rule when replaced or destroyed. The virtual destructor in Estimate lets deletion through the base pointer reach the derived object correctly. These are distinct questions: who can call the object, who controls its release, and how long will it remain alive? Many pattern bugs occur when a diagram explains calls but leaves ownership and lifetime unstated.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

question.prompt: Can storing a reference to a local rule keep that rule alive after its function returns?
question.answer: No. The reference does not extend that local object’s lifetime. Later use would be invalid unless the design keeps the target alive by another means.

opening.title: Move transfers a resource only through a move operation
keyPoints: std::move permits moving; it does not itself transfer
Moving unique_ptr transfers its owned object
The source unique_ptr becomes empty
Do not generalize that empty-state rule to every type
opening.narration: The expression std::move is best read as permission to treat an object as a source for moving. The move constructor or move assignment that receives it performs the actual transfer. When a unique_ptr is moved successfully, the destination becomes the owner and the source becomes empty. That specific rule lets us trace ownership without inventing a second object. Other moved-from library objects have different guarantees, so do not assume that every moved-from value is empty. A design that keeps using the source must respect its documented state. Later patterns use moves to hand completed objects to their caller without copying exclusive owners.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

question.prompt: Does writing std::move(owner) on its own necessarily change owner?
question.answer: No. std::move is a cast-like operation that permits a move. A receiving move operation must perform the transfer.

opening.title: Read a range loop without guessing about punctuation
keyPoints: for visits each element in a range
The colon means “take each element from”
auto infers a type; & borrows; const restricts that access
opening.narration: When you see for followed by const auto ampersand child, a colon, and children, read it as: for each element in children, use a const reference named child. The colon belongs to the range-based for syntax. auto asks the compiler to infer the type; the ampersand avoids making an element copy; const limits modification through that reference. A const unique_ptr still permits changes to the pointed-to object unless the pointed-to type itself is const. Punctuation gets its meaning from context. A colon after a constructor’s parameter list instead begins member initialization, while a colon in a class declaration can introduce base classes.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.08: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles

question.prompt: Does const auto& child make a pointed-to object immutable when child is a unique_ptr?
question.answer: No. It restricts the handle through that reference. The pointed-to type needs its own const qualification to provide a read-only view of the object.

opening.title: Separate what varies from what stays stable
keyPoints: Cohesion: related work belongs together
Coupling: parts rely on an agreement
Isolate evidence of change before creating an extension point
opening.narration: Cohesion asks whether the work inside one part belongs together. Coupling asks how strongly parts rely on each other. Neither word means that a program should contain isolated objects that never communicate. Our estimate callers must agree on inputs and results. The useful aim is a small, clear agreement that changes less often than its implementations. If report colors change for different reasons than temperature calculations, separating those responsibilities can reduce accidental edits. But guessing ten future variants may produce more complexity than the current task needs. Look for repeated edits, duplicated decisions, or a stated need to replace behavior before introducing an extension boundary.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.06: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose

question.prompt: What evidence would justify separating report formatting from alert calculation?
question.answer: Independent requirements or repeated changes to presentation that should not affect which readings count as alerts.

opening.title: Composition keeps independent choices independent
keyPoints: A report has a delivery collaborator
Two report types × three deliveries need not become six subclasses
Inheritance still fits a true substitution promise
opening.narration: Suppose two report formats can each use three delivery methods. A subclass for every pair leads to six combinations, and adding a fourth delivery creates more combinations again. Composition connects a report to a delivery object so each choice can vary separately. In broad design advice, composition can include borrowing a collaborator; in a strict UML composition relationship, the whole also controls its parts’ lifetime. We must therefore inspect the actual ownership rule. Inheritance remains useful when a derived type keeps a base contract or varies a step in a stable workflow. The goal is to match relationships to requirements, not to ban one C++ feature.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.06: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose

question.prompt: Why can composition reduce the number of combined types in the report example?
question.answer: It represents format and delivery as separate choices that are connected at use time, rather than defining a subclass for every pair.

opening.title: Single responsibility means one coherent source of change
keyPoints: Alert policy changes for one reason
Report appearance changes for another
One method per class is not the rule
opening.narration: The Single Responsibility Principle asks us to keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module might be a class or a source file. In our monitor, the alert rule answers whether a reading counts as an alert. A report formatter decides how accepted records appear on screen. A new workshop policy and a new color scheme come from different needs, so combining them can cause unrelated edits and tests to interfere. The principle does not mean every class should have exactly one function. A well-focused class may need several operations to protect the same data and fulfill the same responsibility.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

question.prompt: Would moving every method into a separate class automatically satisfy single responsibility?
question.answer: No. Responsibility is about coherent reasons for change, not a numeric limit on methods.

opening.title: Open/closed protects a planned direction of change
keyPoints: Keep the monitor’s estimate call stable
Add another implementation for a new rule
Selection code still needs to choose the new rule
opening.narration: The Open/Closed Principle asks whether a known extension can be added without repeatedly editing the stable code that uses it. If the monitor calls an Estimate interface, adding another rule can leave its call site unchanged. Some construction or configuration code must still choose the new implementation, and that is acceptable. Closed does not mean no source file may ever change. It means a useful boundary protects one expected direction of change. Fixing a defect or changing the meaning of accepted input may still require editing that boundary. For a tiny fixed set of rules, a direct branch can be clearer than paying for an extension structure nobody needs.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

question.prompt: Does adding a new strategy without editing the monitor prove that no code anywhere changes?
question.answer: No. The new implementation and its selection must be added. The benefit is preserving the agreed stable caller boundary.

opening.title: Substitution is a behavioral promise
keyPoints: A derived type must accept the base’s valid requests
It must keep the base’s result guarantees
Matching C++ syntax is necessary but insufficient
opening.narration: The Liskov Substitution Principle concerns what happens when a caller uses a derived object through a base contract. Suppose Estimate promises to accept every nonempty list of readings in a stated range. A derived implementation that secretly requires ten readings breaks that promise by strengthening the precondition. An implementation that returns a value outside the promised result range weakens the postcondition. Both errors can appear in code that compiles with override. The compiler checks signatures and language rules, while tests and review check units, values, side effects, and other behavioral promises. Run the same contract checks against every implementation, especially the smallest and boundary inputs.
actions: Ask for a prediction before revealing the answer.
Connect the answer to the stated requirement.
opening.sourceRef: content/design-patterns-cpp/ch0.json → C00.07: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design

question.prompt: A derived estimate rejects a one-element list allowed by the base contract. Which promise is broken?
question.answer: It strengthens the precondition, so callers cannot safely substitute it for every valid use of the base interface.

opening.title: Interface segregation follows the caller’s real needs
keyPoints: A reader should not require save or erase
Separate meaningful capabilities
Avoid creating dozens of empty one-method types
opening.narration: The Interface Segregation Principle asks whether callers depend on operations they do not need. An archive reader needs a load operation. If its only available interface also requires save, erase, and network setup, a read-only implementation may have to invent fake operations or throw surprising errors. Splitting reading from writing gives each caller a meaningful promise. One implementation can still support both capabilities. The aim is not the maximum number of tiny interfaces. Excessive splitting can hide which operations belong together. Start by naming the caller’s task, then group the operations needed to complete that task with a clear shared contract.

question.prompt: Why is a read-only implementation whose save method always throws a warning sign?
question.answer: The shared interface may promise capabilities that this implementation cannot meaningfully provide. A separate reading capability can express the actual contract.

opening.title: Dependency inversion protects policy from detail
keyPoints: Policy: decide when an alert is needed
Detail: deliver it to a file or test buffer
Both depend on an appropriate alert-sink contract
opening.narration: The Dependency Inversion Principle concerns the direction of source dependencies. High-level policy says what the program must achieve. A low-level detail says how a device, file, or service carries it out. If alert policy directly depends on a particular file writer, file-format details can spread into the policy. An AlertSink contract can describe the delivery behavior policy needs. The policy depends on that contract, and a file sink or test sink implements it. The contract should express the policy’s need rather than expose every option of one file library. This makes a test implementation possible without making the domain decision about a physical file.

question.prompt: What should an AlertSink interface describe?
question.answer: The delivery behavior and guarantees the policy needs, rather than the incidental API of one file-writing implementation.

opening.title: Injection supplies a collaborator; inversion chooses the dependency
keyPoints: Constructor injection means receiving a needed object
A supplied concrete file writer is still a concrete dependency
The two ideas can work together but are not synonyms
opening.narration: Dependency injection means supplying a needed collaborator from outside instead of constructing it secretly inside the consumer. A constructor parameter is a common way to do this. However, receiving a concrete FileWriter by reference is still a dependency on FileWriter. It is injection, but it does not automatically create dependency inversion. To judge inversion, look at the declared types and what those types promise. A policy receiving an AlertSink can depend on the abstraction while a composition site chooses the actual file sink. That composition site is allowed to know the concrete types because selecting and connecting them is its job.

question.prompt: Is passing a concrete database object into a constructor enough to prove dependency inversion?
question.answer: No. It shows injection. The consumer may still depend directly on the concrete database type and its details.

opening.title: Read class-diagram arrows as specific claims
keyPoints: Hollow triangle points toward a base type
Dependency means uses, not owns
Filled diamond marks composition at the whole
Read the legend before inferring lifetime
opening.narration: A UML class diagram describes types and relationships, not a sequence of calls. In these lessons a solid line with a hollow triangle points from a derived type toward its base. A dashed dependency arrow says that one part uses another. It does not imply ownership. A filled diamond sits at the whole end of a composition relationship. A hollow diamond represents aggregation, but by itself does not specify who deletes a C++ object. Some lesson legends explicitly annotate shared ownership; confirm that claim against the actual owning handles. Teaching connectors join explanatory notes to code and are labeled annotations so they cannot be mistaken for type relationships.

question.prompt: If A has a dashed dependency arrow to B, may you conclude that A destroys B?
question.answer: No. A dependency establishes use. Ownership must be stated separately and supported by the code and diagram legend.

opening.title: Choose the diagram that answers the question
keyPoints: Activity: which branch or action comes next?
Sequence: who calls whom, in time order?
State: which changes are permitted?
Ownership: which event ends an object’s lifetime?
opening.narration: One diagram cannot answer every question equally well. An activity diagram follows possible actions and decisions; its arrows mean execution flow. A sequence diagram puts participants across the page and calls in order down the page. A state diagram shows permitted changes between named states after events. An ownership view makes owners, borrowers, and release events visible. A state diagram does not prove that a program uses the State design pattern: an enum and checked functions can implement the same transition rules. Choose a diagram by the uncertainty you need to resolve, and then verify each arrow against the delivered source rather than treating the picture as evidence by itself.

question.prompt: Which diagram best exposes a listener being called before a publisher returns?
question.answer: A sequence diagram, because it shows participants and the order of calls over time. Ownership still needs separate explanation if listeners are retained.

opening.title: Trace data, control, ownership, and lifetime separately
keyPoints: Data: arguments, stored values, results
Control: calls, branches, returns
Ownership: responsibility transferred or retained
Lifetime: construction and destruction events
opening.narration: A single call can move control without moving ownership. In the estimate demo, main passes two integer values to the selected rule; the result comes back by value. Control enters the rule’s override and returns to main. The unique_ptr remains the owner throughout that call. Replacement is different: it changes which rule is owned and destroys the old one. Lifetime ends at destruction, not merely when an arrow in a call diagram returns. Following these four paths separately prevents the common mistake of assuming that a caller owns every object it uses or that a returned reference keeps its target alive.

question.prompt: During rule->value(1, 9), does ownership move from main to the member function?
question.answer: No. The call transfers control and passes values. The owning pointer remains in main unless an explicit ownership operation says otherwise.

opening.title: Compilation and execution establish different facts
keyPoints: Compile: syntax, access, type compatibility
Link: required definitions can be resolved
Run: values follow the required behavior
A successful build is evidence, not a correctness proof
opening.narration: Compilation checks names, syntax, access rules, and many type relationships. It can reject an override whose signature does not match the base operation. Linking combines compiled pieces and may fail when a required definition is missing. Execution chooses branches for actual values, creates objects, calls functions, and destroys them. The stale report demo passes the build stages yet gives the wrong answer for the highest request. A virtual call’s required behavior is runtime selection of the final override, even when optimization can determine the target earlier. Keep the evidence precise: a successful build proves that this toolchain accepted the program, not that the program meets every requirement.

question.prompt: Would a wrong Fahrenheit-to-Celsius formula necessarily cause a compiler error?
question.answer: No. The formula can be well-typed and syntactically valid. Value-based tests and reasoning must detect the wrong result.

opening.title: Tests should challenge the promise, not just the happy path
keyPoints: Check ordinary inputs and exact outputs
Check boundaries and rejected requests
Verify state is unchanged after promised rejection
Test lifetime and replacement when the pattern depends on them
opening.narration: A test is most useful when it can catch a plausible incorrect implementation. An estimate test should distinguish the mean from the highest reading, rather than use two equal readings that both rules answer the same way. A replacement test should check both before and after the change. A rejection test should verify not only that an error appears, but also that any promised unchanged state really stays unchanged. Where ownership matters, observe a real destruction event with a valid lifetime-safe test. These checks provide evidence for the cases they cover. They do not prove every possible execution, every allocator failure, or every platform behavior.

question.prompt: Why are inputs 5 and 5 weak for distinguishing Mean from Highest?
question.answer: Both return 5, so a test could pass even if the wrong implementation was selected. Inputs 1 and 9 distinguish them.

opening.title: Build one complete demo; know which version you ran
keyPoints: Use the displayed source and explicit language standard
Inspect compiler status before running
Compare stdout, stderr, and exit status
The lecture demos are independent C++20 programs
opening.narration: Each runnable lecture demonstration is a complete source file, with its own main function and expected output. Build and run it separately rather than joining multiple files that each define main. The original chapter companions select C++17; these added lecture demos use an explicit C++20 mode and remain focused on the same mechanisms. Warnings are useful evidence about suspicious code. A failed build must not be followed blindly by an old executable with the same name. Compare the actual output, error stream, and exit code with the stated expectation. The larger companion checks include threading support where needed, such as the Singleton lesson.

question.prompt: Why can seeing the expected output after a failed build be misleading?
question.answer: The command may have run an older executable. Establish that the new build succeeded before treating the run as evidence about the edited source.

opening.title: Study Studio: turn watching into retrieval practice
keyPoints: Outline keeps the problem, examples, and explanation together
Slides support prediction and presenter discussion
Flashcards, scenarios, and labs test different skills
Notes should record the invariant and your reason
opening.narration: Use the chapter tools for different jobs. Start in Outline to identify the problem and the baseline. In Slides, pause before each run and say what you expect; open presenter notes for a fuller explanation. Use the UML views to verify relationships against code. Flashcards help retrieve terms and short decisions, while scenarios ask you to choose and explain a design. Coding Lab requires a working change that passes checks. In your notes, record the condition that must stay true and why your repair preserves it. Re-reading the same answer until it feels familiar is weaker evidence than producing an explanation before revealing the answer.

question.prompt: What should you do immediately before revealing a trace answer?
question.answer: Predict the result and explain the call or state sequence that leads to it. Then compare the explanation as well as the final value.

opening.title: Practice grows from a small edit to defended integration
keyPoints: Modify → trace → repair → compare
Extend while keeping earlier checks
Explain the design in plain words
Capstone: select boundaries that cooperate
opening.narration: The exercise progression makes each new demand visible. A guided edit checks whether you can locate the right part. A trace checks whether you understand execution without relying on the compiler to explain it. A repair asks you to identify the earliest broken promise. A design comparison tests whether you can choose among reasonable alternatives. An extension then requires new behavior while preserving earlier checks. Finally, explain the decision in plain words: what changes, what stays stable, and what cost you accept. The capstone joins these skills around one contract. It does not ask you to insert every pattern into the same program.

question.prompt: Why keep the old tests while implementing an extension?
question.answer: They protect established behavior. Passing only new tests could hide regressions in earlier contracts.

opening.title: Before Chapter 1: defend a simple decision
keyPoints: Two fixed output choices may need one branch
A new rule can justify a replaceable operation
A valid override can still break a contract
Next: a workflow whose creation step must vary
opening.narration: Finish Class 0 by answering three questions without reading a definition. If a small program has two fixed output choices and no extension requirement, why might one switch be a good design? If users must add and replace calculations, what specific responsibility should become interchangeable? If a derived class compiles with override, what behavioral promises still need checking? These answers connect design restraint, variation, and correctness. Chapter 1 starts from a shared job whose record creation must vary. We will meet Factory Method only after that pressure is clear. Carry forward the central habit: explain the problem first, trace the mechanism, and judge the result against its promises.

question.prompt: What is the best short explanation of a successful pattern choice?
question.answer: This requirement makes this responsibility vary; this arrangement localizes that change while preserving these specific invariants and accepting these stated costs.
